video_title: Can the Stock Market Survive a Tech Meltdown? | WAYT?
gist: Michael Batnick and Chart Kid Matt dissect a post-election tech/semis crash (semis down ~30%, Nvidia ~30% off highs amid a Mega Speed controversy) while six S&P sectors sit near highs and S&P 493 earnings revisions outpace the Mag 7. Dot-com history shows non-tech stocks can thrive when tech busts, and Nasdaq-catch-up and CPI-reaction studies offer a constructive base case.

themes.theme: Election shock and AI build-out repricing

insights.claim: After the election results pointed to a Democratic wave expected to slow the AI data-center build-out, Nasdaq 100 futures fell about 3% overnight before reversing to bright green as the narrative flipped to 'slower capex is good'.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Policy risk to AI capex is now a direct driver of index futures; watch political headlines for capex-sensitive names.

insights.claim: The market's reframing was that a slower AI build-out could be bullish because investors already disliked hyperscalers' negative free cash flow, equity issuance, circular financing and strained debt-market access, while end demand was not slowing.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A capex slowdown could be read as balance-sheet relief for hyperscalers rather than purely negative; supplier names bear the downside.
insights.quote: if we have an opportunity to maybe take our foot off of 150 mile an hour gas pedal and we can prolong this over a shorter period of a longer period of time, then that would be good for the market

insights.claim: The Wednesday-Thursday post-election selloff saw 57 S&P 500 stocks fall more than 10% in two days, matching the Liberation Day tariff blow-up, with 32 of the 57 from tech and 12 from industrials.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Breadth of damage was concentrated in tech/AI supply chain, signaling a sector-specific rather than market-wide liquidation.

insights.claim: Thursday's intraday action looked like forced liquidation, falling tick after tick and closing near the lows, a move Batnick said he could not explain fundamentally.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Possible deleveraging/positioning unwind rather than new information; such moves can mean-revert.
insights.quote: it just looked like someone was getting liquidated all day

insights.claim: Micron fell about 23% in the two-day selloff while Nvidia, down about 12% (9% then 3%), was a relative outperformer among semiconductors despite being at the center of the AI build-out narrative.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Memory names carried the highest beta to AI capex fears; Nvidia's relative resilience is notable given its market cap.

insights.claim: Per Rob Anderson of Ned Davis Research, this is the sixth Nasdaq selloff of more than 9% since the 2020 low; outside Liberation Day max drawdowns were around 13%, while the current semiconductor drawdown of about 29% matches Liberation Day.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Semis are experiencing a crash-level drawdown even though the broad index is not.

insights.claim: Unlike prior selloffs where there was nowhere to hide, this one featured strong rotation: insurance stocks gained 13%, pharmaceuticals 10%, staples 15% and commercial and professional services 18% over the same period.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Defensive and non-tech groups are absorbing flows; diversified portfolios are cushioned.
insights.quote: There was plenty of rotation, plenty of places to to make money in the current in the current sell-off.

insights.claim: Six of the S&P 500 sectors were within 3% of all-time highs, including healthcare and staples, despite semiconductors being down roughly 30%.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Negativity is concentrated in tech/semis; sector leadership elsewhere suggests rotation rather than a broad bear market.
insights.quote: there's six sectors within 3% of an all-time [snorts] high

insights.claim: Semiconductors, the largest S&P industry group, fell about 30% while the S&P 500's max drawdown was only about 6%, which Batnick attributes to the sheer amount of money in the system cushioning markets - though he notes there is a limit.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Liquidity is dampening index-level drawdowns, but cap-weighted exposure to AI still caps how much pain the index can absorb.

insights.claim: Index investors are doing fine, but anyone holding concentrated positions outside a cap-weighted index - for example in Google, which got hit hard - is feeling meaningful pain.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Dispersion is high; stock pickers in mega-cap tech are absorbing the damage.

insights.claim: For the current quarter, blended estimates show the S&P 493 growing earnings 32.6% year over year versus 22.6% for the Mag 7 - the first quarter of the past four in which the 493 are expected to outgrow the Mag 7.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Supports the broadening thesis; equal-weight and non-mega-cap exposure has fundamental backing.

insights.claim: Matt attributes part of the 493's earnings surge to energy and part to AI-driven cost cutting filtering into earnings of non-hyperscaler companies.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: AI adopters, not just builders, may be starting to show margin benefits.

insights.claim: The ratio of S&P 493 to Mag 7 forward EPS bottomed on August 31 and is up 6.5% since, while the 493/Mag 7 price ratio is up 7.3% since its October low - the 493's outperformance is backed by faster upward earnings revisions.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Relative earnings-revision ratios are a useful tool to validate rotation trades rather than relying on price alone.
insights.quote: there's actual earnings to back up the story of the 493 in the broadening

insights.claim: Forward earnings estimates update daily as analysts revise projections, whereas trailing earnings update only quarterly, making forward EPS a real-time gauge of fundamental momentum.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Track forward EPS revisions daily to spot turns before quarterly reports.

insights.claim: In Q3, four of six Mag 7 companies that reported beat bottom-line estimates, yet on average fell 3% the next day - contrary to the typical post-beat rally seen since Q1 2018.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Selling on strong beats is a classic warning sign of exhaustion in leadership names.

insights.claim: Both hosts agree that mega-caps falling on big earnings beats is a clear point for the bears, not something to spin positively.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Treat 'beat and sell' reactions as a yellow light for mega-cap tech exposure.
insights.quote: This is this is one for the bears.

insights.claim: Despite the selloff, Nvidia's forward earnings estimates hit an all-time high on the Friday before, meaning analysts had not yet cut numbers.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Watch for estimate cuts; the stock is highly sensitive to even small earnings revisions.

insights.claim: Because Nvidia's price is so sensitive to earnings growth, a modest cut in estimates (e.g., 6%) could produce a far larger stock decline (e.g., 40%), Batnick argued hypothetically.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Earnings-revision risk is asymmetric for high-expectation growth stocks.

insights.claim: Since ChatGPT's launch, Nvidia's forward earnings are up about 3,246% (roughly 30x) while the stock is up about 944% (roughly 9x), meaning earnings growth has far outpaced price.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Valuation has compressed materially; the stock trades on far cheaper multiples than its run implies.

insights.claim: Back-testing Nvidia's forward estimates against realized results since 2021 shows actual trailing 12-month earnings came in above year-ago estimates almost every quarter since 2024, countering claims that forward numbers are inflated.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Analyst estimates for Nvidia have historically been conservative, not inflated - supports the valuation case if the track record holds.

insights.claim: Batnick called Nvidia the 'fattest pitch in the market' the prior Tuesday at roughly 14 times forward earnings, and it has since fallen to perhaps 13 times or lower.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Nvidia at ~13-14x forward earnings is a value-like multiple, but carries risk of being a value trap if estimates fall.
insights.quote: I'm the dumb ass that called it the fattest pitch in the market last Tuesday

insights.claim: Nvidia went from an all-time high about a month earlier to roughly 30% off its high in around 25 trading sessions, with the stock falling a further ~6% on the recording day.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Speed of the drawdown is extreme for the world's largest stock.

themes.theme: Nvidia key-man and Mega Speed risk

insights.claim: Short seller Culper Research flagged on May 13 a close relationship between Nvidia's CEO and Mega Speed's Alice Wong - partying together in June 2024 and dining in May 2025 just after US trade restrictions - well before the story broke; the stock is now down about 20% since.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Short-seller research on governance/export-control links can front-run major stock-moving news.

insights.claim: The New York Times reported on the CEO/Mega Speed story about a week earlier without moving the stock; the market only reacted once the CEO emailed his team, indicating narrative timing matters more than information release.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Markets can ignore public negative news until a catalyst crystallizes it; watch for regulatory or congressional follow-through.

insights.claim: Batnick ranks Jensen as the number-two key-man risk among mega-cap CEOs after Elon Musk, saying if anything bad happens to him, Nvidia stock is going way lower.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Leadership/legal risk at Nvidia is now a live tail risk not captured in earnings models.
insights.quote: outside of Elon Musk, I would think that Jensen is number two for key man risk

themes.theme: Value vs growth and index construction

insights.claim: The Russell 1000 value vs growth ratio (IWD vs growth) is at a three-year high, value just had its best six-day outperformance since 2000, yet the ratio is unchanged since mid-2020.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Value's sharp outperformance resembles a dot-com-style unwind signal but has repeatedly faked out before.

insights.claim: Value can only keep outperforming growth if the AI trade has peaked; the two cannot both continue, and Batnick does not believe the AI trade has peaked.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Value-vs-growth positioning is effectively a bet on whether the AI trade has topped.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 Value index's largest sector is technology, with financials 15%, healthcare 13% and staples only 8.5%, and S&P can split a single stock's weight between the growth and value indexes.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: 'Value' indexes may carry substantial tech/AI exposure; check constituents before using them as an AI hedge.

insights.claim: Top holdings of the S&P value index include names like Tesla and Apple, which are hardly value stocks by multiple, and Intel is still up about 60% year to date.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Style labels can be misleading; value funds may not diversify away from mega-cap risk.

insights.claim: Value ETF returns diverge enormously: VLUE (iShares MSCI USA Value Factor, with Micron as its largest holding) is up 37% year to date versus IVE up 14%, a spread of over 20 points.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Which value ETF you choose matters hugely - VLUE carries semiconductor exposure that recently got crushed.
insights.quote: It matters what you choose. You got to look at the actual constituents.

insights.claim: Twenty-four months after the dot-com peak, 129 S&P 500 stocks were up more than 50% - more than the number down 50% at that time.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: A tech peak does not imply a broad market wipeout; many non-tech stocks thrived.

insights.claim: From March 2000 to the October 2002 bottom, tech and communication services fell 70% while the rest of the market was up 3%, and before the final capitulation the rest of the market had been up almost 40%.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: If AI/tech has peaked, the historical template favors the non-tech 493 strongly.
insights.quote: Everything else was actually up from the dot com peak to the absolute low of the dot com bubble.

insights.claim: During the dot-com bust, 99% of tech stocks entered a bear market, but only about a third of staples, financials and utilities names fell 20%, and only 45% of materials stocks did.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Defensive and financial sectors offered substantial protection in a tech-led bust.

insights.claim: About 50% of financials and consumer discretionary stocks were higher at the 2002 market bottom than at the 2000 peak.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Broad sector baskets can deliver positive returns through a tech bear market.

insights.claim: The dot-com bust was a stock-market recession rather than a deep economic recession, so the favorable outcome for non-tech stocks depends on avoiding a massive global recession this time.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: The broadening playbook breaks down if a tech bust spills into a real economic recession.
insights.quote: It was a stock market recession. It was not an economic catastrophe.

insights.claim: A visible capitulation spike - stocks down 50%+ surging and stocks up 50%+ collapsing - marked the dot-com low, though such signals are only clear in hindsight.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Breadth capitulation can help identify bottoms but is easily mistaken in real time.

themes.theme: Signals: Nasdaq catch-up, CPI reaction, MSCI

insights.claim: When the equal-weight S&P 500 hits a new high while the Nasdaq 100 is 10% off its high, the Nasdaq 100 historically catches up rather than equal-weight catching down, averaging +8.1% after 3 months and +21.6% after 12 months excluding the tech bubble.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Historical base rate favors buying Nasdaq 100 weakness when equal-weight is at highs; expected recovery to new highs ~113 trading days.

insights.claim: A hot month-over-month CPI print (no year-over-year figure available due to last October's government shutdown) pushed Fed funds futures for early 2028 from 4.37% to 4.54%, implying rate hikes are being priced.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Markets are pricing a rising policy rate path; rate-sensitive assets and the two-year yield are vulnerable.

insights.claim: When stocks rise on a hotter-than-expected CPI print, the S&P 500 has averaged a 6.2% gain over the next three months and been positive 91% of the time; when stocks fall on a cold CPI, it averaged +5.5%.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: Trade the market's reaction to data rather than the data itself - resilience to bad news is a bullish signal.

insights.claim: In 2026 the cap-weighted market is so top-heavy and AI-driven that index moves, like the CPI-day decline with Nvidia down 6%, can have nothing to do with the macro data.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Macro-reaction signals on the cap-weighted index are distorted; use equal-weight for cleaner reads.

insights.claim: Matt makes the bull case for MSCI as an AI-era data provider: the stock has based since late 2021/early 2022, revenue has tripled since 2015, operating margin hit 56% TTM, and a breakout above about $700 could quickly take it toward $1,000.
insights.speaker: Matt (Chart Kid Matt)
insights.so_what: MSCI is a technical breakout candidate with strong fundamentals; a trend-line break would signal exit.
insights.quote: if it breaks out, I think above let's just use 700. This thing could go to like $1,000 really quick

insights.claim: The selloff in data providers and rating agencies like FactSet on fears of AI disruption is misguided because they are regulated, decades-built franchises that AI tools like Claude cannot simply replicate, and partnerships are more likely.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: AI-disruption fears in data/index providers may create buying opportunities.

insights.claim: XRT retail stocks, which badly lagged the S&P 500 into October and prompted recession worries, are now outperforming over the last year, but Batnick argues retail and equal-weight discretionary have trended down for years and their moves say nothing about the economy.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Don't read macro signals into retail-stock breakdowns or recoveries.
insights.quote: it's been going down until the right for years
